name: pp-wave Plane Gravitational Waves
description: A class of exact solutions describing gravitational waves with plane fronts and parallel rays. They model the radiation field of rapidly moving sources and exact gravitational wave geometries.
history: H. W. Brinkmann was not looking for a gravitational wave. In 1925, asking which Einstein spaces can be mapped conformally onto one another, he was handed a family of metrics carrying a null vector field parallel to itself everywhere [brinkmann1925]. He did not call them waves. Nobody did for thirty six years, until Kundt and Ehlers named them the plane-fronted waves with parallel rays [kundt1961, ehlerskundt1962]. Physics had spent those decades on something more basic, and Eddington had set the terms in 1923: the potentials answer to the coordinate system as much as to the geometry, so that one can, in his phrase, propagate coordinate changes with the speed of thought [eddington1923]. The cure he named in the same breath, a curvature invariant in place of a potential, he left to somebody else.¶Einstein nearly talked the waves out of existence. In 1936 he told Max Born he had reached the interesting result that gravitational waves do not exist, and sent the argument, with Nathan Rosen, to Physical Review. The editor, John Tate, passed it to a referee, who returned a long list of objections. Einstein, unused to being refereed, pulled the paper: he saw no reason, he wrote, to address the in any case erroneous comments of the journal's anonymous expert. He never published there again. Leopold Infeld, Rosen's replacement, then read the manuscript with a friendly local relativist; the singularity that had killed the wave sat on the axis of the cylindrical coordinates and nowhere else. It ran in 1937 in the Journal of the Franklin Institute, conclusion reversed, with a note thanking Professor Robertson for his friendly help [einstein1937]. Robertson was the referee, which Einstein appears never to have learned [kennefick2005].¶Whether the waves carry energy outlasted Einstein, and was settled in a single week in North Carolina. Felix Pirani supplied the tool in 1956: what a wave does to two freely falling particles is fixed by the Riemann tensor through the equation of geodesic deviation, and the Riemann tensor cares nothing for coordinates [pirani1956]. Eddington's cure, thirty three years late. Pirani's paper appeared in Acta Physica Polonica because he had gone to Warsaw to visit Infeld, stripped of his Canadian citizenship for going home to rebuild Polish physics. At Chapel Hill in January 1957 Bondi asked from the floor whether the thing could be made into an absorber of gravitational energy; Pirani had put in no absorption term, only a spring. Feynman supplied the friction: let one mass carry a stick running past touching a second, the wave slides the second along the stick, the rubbing makes heat, and heat is energy [feynman2011]. He had hesitated to say any of it, having missed the session on gravitational waves entirely.¶Bondi came to that conference a skeptic and left converted, and within months had a version of the argument in Nature [bondi1957]. In 1959, with Pirani and Ivor Robinson, he gave the exact plane waves their full treatment: the most symmetric members of Brinkmann's family, five Killing vectors apiece and no singularity in them [bondipirani1959]. Thirty four years on, a curiosity of conformal geometry was a gravitational wave. Joseph Weber, also in that audience, went home to Maryland and built the first antenna out of a large aluminum cylinder [weber1960]. His detections did not survive scrutiny; the enterprise did. The binary pulsar Hulse and Taylor found in 1974 was losing orbital period at exactly the rate a radiating system should [hulse1975, taylor1979], and on 14 September 2015 two detectors caught the same fifth of a second of chirp [abbott2016]. LIGO is Feynman's stick at scale, with hanging mirrors for the rubbing masses and a laser where the friction was, and what sweeps through it is, to any accuracy the instrument can tell, one of Brinkmann's metrics.
